The first thing that comes is the hum of the refrigerator, a low note that has been there all along, waiting for silence to notice it. Then the clock ticking, though it’s digital and doesn’t tick; still, I hear a tick, because the mind insists on rhythm, on measuring the unmeasurable. The screen is white, or nearly white, a field of snow that isn’t cold. A cursor blinks. It is a tiny heartbeat, a metronome for thought. I have a thousand words, which is both a lot and almost nothing. A thousand words is a long letter, a short story, a confession, a rant, a prayer. It is enough to say I was here, and not enough to say everything.

I think about all the words I’ve swallowed. The ones that sat in my throat like stones, smooth and heavy. Apologies I never made. Compliments I thought but didn’t speak. Questions that might have changed things. Words are strange creatures. They can build a bridge or a wall, and often we don’t know which until we’ve crossed or been turned away. I used to believe that if I could just find the right sentence, I could fix something. Now I think the right sentence is mostly a hand held out, not a key. It doesn’t unlock the door; it says, I am here on the other side, and I don’t know either.

Rain begins. Not real rain—maybe real, I can’t tell from inside—but in memory it begins. I am eight years old, sitting on the porch of a house that no longer exists, watching water fall from the eaves in silver ropes. My grandmother is inside, humming a hymn I will forget and then remember decades later in a grocery store aisle, of all places, between the rice and the canned tomatoes. She had hands that could make dough feel like forgiveness. She never said “I love you” directly, but she said “Eat something” and “You’re cold” and “Sit by me.” I am beginning to understand that love is often a translation problem. We say one thing and mean another, and if we’re lucky, someone hears the meaning anyway.

What else comes? A dog I had as a boy, a mutt with one ear up and one ear down, as if he couldn’t decide whether to listen or not. He is running in a field in a season I can’t name. The grass is high and green and then gold. He is always running toward me, but he never arrives. That’s memory for you: a loop of almost. Maybe that’s why I write. To let the dog arrive. To let the rain finish. To let the words I swallowed find a mouth.

Outside the window, a stranger passes. I don’t know their name, their worries, whether they are happy or just walking. They are carrying a bag of groceries. A leek sticks out like a green flag. For a second, we are connected by the absurd fact of a leek. Then they are gone. This is the city: a thousand lives brushing against each other like pages in a book that never quite opens. I want to write them all. The woman with the leek. The man who laughs too loudly on the bus. The child who asks “why” until the adult runs out of answers. Everyone is a universe with a heartbeat, and we pass each other like ships in the night, blinking our lights.

I think about the internet, that vast ocean of words. We are all shouting into it, hoping someone will hear. Sometimes someone does. A stranger likes a post. A comment says “me too.” And for a moment, the loneliness lifts like fog. But then the scroll continues, and we are alone again, surrounded by the digital ghosts of everyone we’ve never met. I don’t know if this is good or bad. Maybe it’s just human. We have always wanted to be heard. We have always wanted to be known. The tools change; the hunger doesn’t.

Time is a river, they say. I used to think I was on the bank, watching it go. Now I think I am the river, and the bank is made of moments. The past is not behind me; it is inside me, a sediment. The future is not ahead; it is the next bend. I am carrying all the versions of myself downstream—the child, the teenager, the person who made mistakes, the person who tried again. They are all still here, arguing, singing, sleeping. I can’t leave them behind. I can only give them a seat in the boat.

Maybe that’s what writing is: a boat. You put the things you can’t carry alone into it, and you push off. You don’t know where you’re going. You just know that the water is deep and dark and full of stars. You row. You sing. You fall silent. You listen to the hum of the refrigerator. You notice the cursor. You notice the rain. You notice the leek. You notice the dog who never arrives. And you keep going, because there is nothing else to do, and because somewhere in the accumulation of small, ordinary words, something true might surface. Not a grand truth. Not the meaning of life. Just a truth: I was here. I noticed. I tried. I loved, imperfectly. I failed, honestly. I hoped.

A thousand words. I have used most of them. Not all. There are a few left, and they are yours. Take them. Use them for something kind. Write a note to someone you miss. Say the thing you swallowed. Let the dog arrive. Let the rain finish. Let the leek be a flag for all of us, waving from a grocery bag, ridiculous and holy. The cursor blinks. The hum continues. The world is full of endings, but this is not one. This is just a pause. The next word is waiting. I’ll meet you there.
